summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for agreeing how a formfeed character in output is handled. A formfeed traditionally tells a printer or terminal to start a new page or clear the screen. The option lets the two ends settle that between them. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A formfeed is the signal for starting a fresh page. This note lets two computers agree on what to do when that signal arrives.

subtitle: Negotiating how to handle formfeed characters in Telnet output.

tldr.problem: A formfeed character (ASCII 12) tells a printer or terminal to advance to a new page or clear the screen. When sent over Telnet, the two sides need to agree on how it is handled.
tldr.mechanism: The option follows the same pattern as the horizontal tab disposition option (RFC 654): the sender and receiver negotiate via Telnet commands, choosing from eight strategies—pass it through, replace it with line-feeds, discard it, simulate it, delay after it, or wait for a response.
tldr.outcome: Both sides know how formfeed characters will be processed. The RFC is Historic and formfeed is rarely used in modern systems.

today: RFC 655 is Historic and formfeed characters are rarely used in modern Telnet or terminal applications. Modern systems typically do not support formfeed at all or treat it as a simple control character.

sections.title: The Telnet Formfeed Disposition Option
sections.content: RFC 655 defines the NAOFFD option (Negotiate About Output Formfeed Disposition), a Telnet option for handling the formfeed character when it appears in output. On old printers and terminals, a formfeed (ASCII 12) means "advance to the top of the next page" or "clear the screen." Different systems interpret formfeed differently, so the two ends of a Telnet connection need to negotiate how it will be handled.
sections.plainLanguage: Formfeed is the signal for a new page or a clear screen. This option lets two computers agree on what to do with it.

sections.title: Formfeed Disposition Strategies
sections.content:
Like RFC 654, this option defines eight strategies, encoded as values 0 to 255. A value of 0 means the sender will handle the formfeed. Values 1 to 250 mean the receiver should handle it with a delay (the value is the number of NUL characters to insert after the formfeed). Value 251 means replace the formfeed with carriage-return/line-feed. Value 252 means discard the formfeed entirely. Value 253 means simulate the formfeed by inserting enough line-feeds to reach the top of the next page. Value 254 means wait for a character on the opposite connection. Value 255 means the receiver should decide.

The guiding principle is that if both sides want to handle formfeeds, the sender wins. If neither wants to, the receiver must handle it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eight choices: I will handle it (0); you handle it with a delay (1-250); replace with line-feeds (251); discard (252); simulate it (253); wait for the other direction (254); or you decide (255).

sections.title: The Negotiation Process
sections.content: The negotiation uses the standard Telnet option protocol. Both sides exchange DO/WILL and DON'T/WON'T commands to agree on whether to negotiate. Once agreed, they use subnegotiation (IAC SB NAOFFD DS or IAC SB NAOFFD DR) to propose their preferred disposition value. The data sender uses code DS (1) and the receiver uses code DR (0). Once both sides agree, the chosen strategy is applied to every formfeed character until renegotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The two computers use standard Telnet negotiation commands, agree on a formfeed strategy, and then apply it to every formfeed character.
